analysis.one_liner: Raises fines on health plans and insurers that violate surprise-billing protections or pay providers late.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final two weeks of the 118th Congress, sent to the Senate HELP Committee, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would crack down on health insurers and employer health plans that break the No Surprises Act, the law that shields patients from surprise out-of-network medical bills. It would raise the fine for each violation from $100 to up to $10,000, make plans pay nonparticipating providers three times the shortfall plus interest when they pay late or not at all after a dispute ruling, and require twice-yearly public reports on audits and enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: People with health insurance who are supposed to be protected from surprise out-of-network bills but end up with them anyway when their plan ignores the rules, and out-of-network doctors, hospitals, and air ambulance operators who wait months for payments that dispute rulings already awarded them. Patients benefit directly from stronger enforcement of balance-billing protections, and the late-payment penalties plus interest go to providers who were underpaid or unpaid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with surprise bills and unpaid providers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty for a group health plan or insurer that violates the No Surprises Act's core balance-billing protections from $100 per failure to $10,000 per failure, under the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the tax code alike.

Adds a new financial penalty for plans that pay late or not at all after an independent dispute resolution decision: three times the difference between the initial payment (or zero, if the plan denied payment) and the awarded out-of-network rate, plus interest.

Requires the agencies to report to Congress every six months on audits conducted, complaints filed by providers and by patients, enforcement actions, civil money penalties issued, and the three most common violations — replacing an annual count of audits only.
Creates a paper trail: plans must notify the Secretary when they make a payment ordered by a dispute-resolution entity, so failures to comply can be detected and penalized.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and group health plans, including self-funded employer plans, that violate the balance-billing rules or delay payments after a dispute ruling. Plans would face up to $10,000 per violation instead of $100, plus triple-difference payments and interest for late or missing payments. Because employer plans are funded by employers and workers' premiums, some of that exposure could ultimately show up in health benefit costs.

drawbacks.text: The triple-difference late-payment penalty is paid to the nonparticipating provider or facility, not to the patient who was stuck in the middle; patients get enforcement indirectly rather than compensation.

Heavier penalty exposure falls on group health plans generally, including employer plans that fund coverage with worker premiums, so some compliance costs could flow back into what employers and employees pay for insurance.

Penalties and interest enrich out-of-network providers and facilities, including air ambulance operators, giving providers on the winning side of disputes a larger financial stake in enforcement outcomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — making an existing patient protection real instead of nominal — is significant, since the current $100-per-violation penalty gives plans little reason to comply and unpaid providers often pass costs back to patients or pursue them in collections. The main costs fall on noncompliant plans rather than on the public, though some could reach premiums, and the fact that the money flows to providers rather than patients means the remedy is indirect. On balance, a well-aimed enforcement bill whose cost is borne mostly by the parties breaking the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 18 days left in the Congress, referred to the Senate health committee, and never heard from again; the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Marshall introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, with Senator Michael Bennet as the sole cosponsor, giving it one Republican and one Democratic sponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; that was the last recorded action of any kind.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, the Senate never voted, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 — eighteen days after introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and group health plans: they keep operating under the current $100-per-violation penalty, which is small enough that violating the surprise-billing and prompt-payment rules carries little financial risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and plans that under-enforced rules

for.name: Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan two-sponsor effort.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote; the bill never left the committee.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no recorded opposition; the bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, so its support was bipartisan but extremely thin.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans (including self-funded employer plans)
industries.note: The bill raises the price of breaking surprise-billing rules from $100 per violation to up to $10,000, and adds triple-difference payments plus interest for slow or missing payments after dispute rulings. Insurers and plans benefit from the status quo, where weak penalties make noncompliance cheap; that cost lands on patients who get billed anyway and on providers left unpaid.

industries.industry: Out-of-network providers, facilities, and air ambulance operators
industries.note: Nonparticipating providers and facilities would receive triple the shortfall plus interest when plans pay late or deny payment after a dispute ruling, and stronger enforcement means they get paid the rates already awarded. Patients gain from the same enforcement, so the industry's interest here runs alongside theirs, though the money goes to providers rather than to patients.
